analysis.one_liner: Bars hospitals from forcing nurses to work beyond 12-hour shifts, with fines for violators.
analysis.headline: Kennedy's bill to stop hospitals from forcing nurses past 12-hour shifts, backed by 13 Senate Democrats, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended Medicare rules to bar hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other Medicare providers from forcing a nurse to work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 12 hours in a 24-hour period, or more than 80 hours in 14 days — with an exception only for officially declared emergencies. It also would have protected nurses from retaliation for refusing or reporting forced overtime, and let the government fine violators up to $10,000 per offense and publish their names. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses at Medicare-participating hospitals, hospital outpatient departments, critical access hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and similar providers. They could no longer be required to work beyond 12 hours in a day or 80 in 14 days except during a declared emergency, and they would gain whistleblower protections, a complaint process with HHS, required posting of schedules and rights notices, and protection from being reported to state licensing boards for refusing forced overtime. Patients also benefit, since the bill's stated purpose is to reduce care delivered by fatigued nurses.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits Medicare providers from requiring a nurse to work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 12 hours in a 24-hour period, or more than 80 hours in a consecutive 14-day period, with an exception only during a declared state of emergency.

Defines 'mandatory overtime' to include any request a nurse cannot refuse without facing discharge, discipline, loss of promotion, or a report to the state licensing board, and expressly excludes chronic understaffing and labor disputes from the emergency exception.

Gives nurses the right to file complaints with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, requires investigation, and bans providers from penalizing or retaliating against nurses who refuse forced overtime or report violations.
Authorizes civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, higher penalties for patterns of repeat violations, and public posting of penalized providers' names on the HHS website.

Requires the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality to study and recommend safe maximum nursing work hours, and OMB to report on federally operated medical facilities (VA, Defense Department) whose overtime practices conflict with the new rules.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and other Medicare providers of services. They would lose mandatory overtime as a staffing tool and would have to hire enough nurses — or pay for voluntary overtime — to cover shifts, with fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation, steeper penalties for repeat offenders, and public listing of violators on a federal website as added pressure. Those staffing costs would ultimately flow into provider finances and Medicare payment negotiations.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals facing real nursing shortages would have to cover shifts another way; because the emergency exception excludes 'consistent understaffing,' a facility that cannot hire enough nurses would have to pay more for voluntary overtime or agency staff, or reduce services — costs that could push up health care prices and Medicare spending.

The bill itself left the central question unsettled: it ordered a government study, due two years after enactment, on what maximum work hours actually protect patient safety, rather than setting the standard from the start.
It relies on HHS enforcement — complaint procedures, investigations, and penalties — so its strength would depend on how aggressively the department of the day policed violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a documented problem: nurses working fatigued on extended shifts, contributing to medical errors and driving nurses out of the profession. Nurses keep the right to volunteer for extra hours, and emergencies are still covered by a narrow exception, so the safety cost of the cap is limited. The real cost falls on hospitals that had been using forced overtime to paper over staffing gaps, and on whoever ultimately pays for the additional hiring — plausibly Medicare and insurers. On balance it was a straightforward pro-nurse, pro-patient labor standard whose main weakness was deferring the precise safe-hours number to a future study.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Safe Nursing and Patient Care Act of 2001 on November 14, 2001, joined at introduction by Senators Kerry, Reid, Wellstone, and Clinton.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
Thirteen senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill, but the Finance Committee took no further action on it.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, with the bill still sitting in committee — no vote ever occurred in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and other Medicare providers that rely on mandatory overtime as a staffing method came out ahead — they avoided a federal cap and the associated fines without ever having to fight a floor vote. Nurses and patients gained nothing.

for.name: Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: 13 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

for.name: American Nurses Association
for.role: National nurses' union and professional association
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed federal limits on mandatory overtime for nurses.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Hospital industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal caps on mandatory overtime as an intrusion on hospital staffing decisions.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Senate Democrats — 13 of 49 in the caucus — with no Republican support, and the bill never reached a vote in either chamber.

industries.note: Hospitals would lose the ability to fill staffing gaps by requiring nurses to work past 12 hours a day or 80 hours in 14 days, and would face fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation plus public listing on an HHS website. Their interest in keeping forced overtime available ran directly against the nurses and patients the bill was meant to protect.

industries.industry: Home health agencies, clinics, and other Medicare providers
industries.note: The overtime limits and penalties applied not just to hospitals but to home health agencies, rehabilitation agencies, ambulatory surgical centers, rural health clinics, and federally qualified health centers that participate in Medicare.
